questions.stem: A 49 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 9 years has never attended eye screening. He drives and reads without difficulty. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. Dilated fundoscopy shows scattered microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages and yellow hard exudates away from the macula in both eyes.
questions.q: Which statement best describes his eye condition?
o: Retinopathy is often asymptomatic until it is advanced
These changes are caused by hypertension alone
questions.e: Diabetic retinopathy is a microvascular complication that is often asymptomatic early, which is why screening matters.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which statement best describes his eye condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Clear signs but **perfect vision** = retinopathy is silent early.

elim: Early retinopathy is typically asymptomatic.
It is microvascular.
Microaneurysms in a diabetic indicate diabetic retinopathy.
Moderate NPDR needs monitoring and risk-factor control.

steps.x: **C. Retinopathy is often asymptomatic until it is advanced.** Diabetic retinopathy is often asymptomatic early: screen annually.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 30 years has fundoscopy. There are intraretinal haemorrhages in all four quadrants, venous beading in two quadrants and an intraretinal microvascular abnormality in one quadrant. There are no new vessels. Visual acuity is 6/9 bilaterally.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The 4-2-1 rule (haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, IRMA in 1) without new vessels defines severe NPDR.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
4 + 2 + 1 and **no new vessels** = severe NPDR.

elim: Gives AV nipping and flame haemorrhages, not this 4-2-1 pattern.
Microaneurysms only.
Has haemorrhages and exudates but does not meet the 4-2-1 rule.
Needs new vessels, which are absent.

steps.x: **E. Severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy.** Severe NPDR: 4-2-1 rule.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with type 2 diabetes has retinal screening. Photographs show microaneurysms, a few dot-blot haemorrhages, scattered hard exudates away from the fovea and two fluffy white patches with indistinct edges. There are no new vessels. His vision is 6/6.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the fluffy white patches?
questions.e: Cotton wool spots are areas of retinal infarction from capillary occlusion; with dot-blot haemorrhages and exudates they indicate moderate NPDR.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of the fluffy white patches? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: fluffy white patches with indistinct edges
steps.x: Fluffy white = **cotton wool spot** = nerve fibre layer **infarction**.

elim: Yellow deposits of age-related macular degeneration.
Sharp-edged yellow lipid deposits, also present here but not fluffy.
Congenital, feathery, unrelated to diabetes.
Gives a grey elevated retina with sudden symptoms.

steps.x: **E. Retinal infarction.** Moderate NPDR adds dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and moderate NPDR says her reading vision in the right eye has become blurred over 2 months. She has no floaters. Visual acuity is 6/24 right, 6/9 left. Fundoscopy shows retinal thickening and a ring of hard exudates close to the right fovea.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her reduced vision?
questions.e: Central blur with exudates and thickening at the fovea is diabetic maculopathy (macular oedema), the most common cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her reduced vision? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Central vision + exudates at fovea = **maculopathy**.

elim: Gives new vessels and haemorrhage rather than central thickening.
Sudden curtain over vision.
Sudden floaters and loss of red reflex.
Sudden painless loss with a cherry red spot.

steps.x: **B. Diabetic maculopathy.** Maculopathy is the commonest cause of vision loss in diabetic eye disease.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man with type 1 diabetes has retinal screening. Photographs show fine, looping vessels growing on the surface of the retina along the superior arcade and a small pre-retinal haemorrhage. He reports occasional floaters. Visual acuity is 6/9 both eyes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely screening grade?
questions.e: New vessels on the retina with pre-retinal haemorrhage is active proliferative retinopathy, graded R3A.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely screening grade? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: fine, looping vessels growing on the surface
steps.x: **New vessels** = proliferative = R3; untreated and bleeding = **A** (active).

elim: There is clear pathology.
Microaneurysms only.
No new vessels at R2.
Stable means previously treated and inactive; these vessels are active.

steps.x: **D. R3A proliferative retinopathy.** Grading: R0, R1 mild, R2 moderate/pre-proliferative, R3A active / R3S stable proliferative.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with proliferative diabetic retinopathy wakes with a red haze and many dark streaks across the vision of her left eye. Visual acuity is counting fingers. The red reflex is dull and fundoscopy shows a red opacity obscuring the retina. Her BP is 156/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Fragile new vessels in PDR rupture into the vitreous, causing sudden floaters, dark streaks and a red opacity obscuring the fundus.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely complication? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
PDR + sudden floaters/streaks + no fundal view = **vitreous haemorrhage**.

elim: Painful red eye with a fixed pupil.
Visible stormy fundus with widespread haemorrhages, retina seen.
Gradual central blurring, not sudden red haze.
Flashes and floaters with a clear view of the retina.

steps.x: **E. Vitreous haemorrhage.** Sudden vision loss in a diabetic: vitreous haemorrhage or detachment, an emergency.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and fibrovascular membranes has had a progressive shadow over the upper half of his right visual field for 3 days. Visual acuity is 6/60. Fundoscopy shows a corrugated, grey, elevated area of retina in the inferior half.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fibrovascular proliferation in PDR can pull the retina off (tractional detachment), seen as a serrated grey elevated retina.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Grey, folded retina** + shadow = detachment.

elim: Pale, oedematous segment with sudden loss.
Central blur, not a field shadow.
Painful with RAPD in younger patients.
Red opacity that obscures the fundal view rather than grey retina.

steps.x: **D. Retinal detachment.** Retinal detachment in diabetes: serrated grey retina, needs immediate referral.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 4 years has moderate NPDR on screening, which has progressed rapidly over a year. His HbA1c is 92 mmol/mol (<42), BP 168/98 mmHg and total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L. He has smoked for 30 years.
questions.q: Which factors most likely explain his rapid progression?
questions.e: After duration of diabetes, the main risk factors are poor glycaemic control and hypertension; controlling glucose, BP and lipids slows progression.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which factors most likely explain his rapid progression? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Short duration but fast progression = blame **glucose** and **BP**.

elim: A separate condition.
Myopia is not a risk factor for progression.
Laser slows progression.
Not a risk factor.

steps.x: **C. Poor glycaemic control and hypertension.** Risk factors: duration, then poor glycaemic control and hypertension.

questions.stem: Two patients attend diabetic eye screening on the same day. Patient A is 35 and has had type 1 diabetes for 22 years with HbA1c 55 mmol/mol. Patient B is 60 and has had type 2 diabetes for 2 years with HbA1c 60 mmol/mol. Patient A has more advanced retinopathy.
questions.q: Which factor best explains the difference?
questions.e: The most important risk factor for diabetic retinopathy is duration of diabetes, followed by glycaemic control and hypertension.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which factor best explains the difference? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
22 years vs 2 years = **duration** wins.

elim: The older patient has less disease.
Patient B's HbA1c is higher yet has less retinopathy.
Not the main risk factor.
Both types develop retinopathy; duration matters more.

steps.x: **B. Duration of diabetes.** Duration of diabetes is the most important risk factor.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with type 2 diabetes for 5 years has her retinal photographs reviewed. There are a few tiny red dots at the posterior pole in each eye. There are no haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots or venous changes. Vision is 6/6.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Microaneurysms only is mild NPDR (R1), managed conservatively by risk-factor control with the GP and continued screening.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots
steps.x: Red dots **only** = microaneurysms = mild NPDR.

elim: Arteriolar narrowing, not microaneurysms.
Would show dot-blot haemorrhages, exudates or cotton wool spots.
Needs new vessels.
Bone-spicule pigment, not red dots.

steps.x: **B. Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy.** Mild NPDR: microaneurysms only.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with proliferative diabetic retinopathy has sudden, painless loss of vision in his right eye this morning. Visual acuity is hand movements. The red reflex is absent and the fundus cannot be seen. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most important complication to exclude?
questions.e: Sudden vision loss in a diabetic suggests vitreous haemorrhage with or without detachment; when the fundus is obscured, detachment must be excluded (B-scan).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most important complication to exclude? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Haemorrhage hides the retina, so a **detachment** may be missed.

elim: Painful, with a hazy cornea.
Painful red photophobic eye.
Gradual, not sudden.
Usually with headache and jaw claudication; fundus visible.

steps.x: **E. Retinal detachment.** Haemorrhage + detachment together obscure the view; exclude detachment.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has not attended screening for 5 years. Fundoscopy shows widespread blot haemorrhages and a frond of fine new vessels arising from the optic disc. She has noticed occasional floaters but vision is 6/12.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Neovascularisation, here new vessels at the disc, defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy, with risk of haemorrhage, fibrosis and detachment.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: fine new vessels arising from the optic disc
steps.x: Any **new vessels** = proliferative.

elim: Central exudates and oedema, not disc new vessels.
No new vessels at this stage.
Swollen disc margins, not new vessels.
No new vessels by definition.

steps.x: **D. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy.** PDR: retinal neovascularisation driven by VEGF.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with type 2 diabetes attends his GP with gradually blurred vision in both eyes for 3 months. He has missed his last two screening appointments. His visual acuity is 6/12 in both eyes. The GP has an ophthalmoscope.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: The initial investigation for diabetic eye disease is fundoscopic examination; screening uses annual digital photography.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: missed his last two screening appointments
steps.x: First look at the retina = **fundoscopy**.

Not indicated for bilateral gradual blur.

Used in optic nerve disease.

steps.x: **C. Dilated fundoscopic examination.** Initial investigation: fundoscopy.

questions.stem: A 13 year old boy with type 1 diabetes diagnosed 2 years ago asks how his eyes will be checked. He has no visual symptoms and his acuity is 6/5 in both eyes. His HbA1c is 58 mmol/mol (<42).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: The NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme offers annual digital retinal photography to people with diabetes aged 12 and over.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: how his eyes will be checked
steps.x: Screening = **annual retinal photographs**.

Not a retinopathy screen.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has hard exudates within one disc diameter of the centre of the fovea on her screening photographs (M1). Visual acuity is 6/12 right. The ophthalmologist wants to measure retinal thickness at the macula.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: OCT gives cross-sectional retinal imaging and specifically assesses macular oedema; M1 means clinically significant maculopathy with exudates near the fovea.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: measure retinal thickness at the macula
steps.x: Macular **thickness** = **OCT**.

elim: Shows retinal detachment when the view is obscured.
Measures global retinal function.

steps.x: **D. Optical coherence tomography.** Gold standard: retinal imaging (photography and OCT); OCT for macular oedema.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with severe NPDR has unexplained worsening of vision. The ophthalmologist wants to identify areas of capillary non-perfusion and early neovascularisation to plan laser treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Fluorescein angiography is used in severe disease to evaluate the vasculature, identify ischaemia and neovascularisation and guide treatment.

Map **vessels and ischaemia** = dye study = fluorescein angiography.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with proliferative diabetic retinopathy has sudden loss of vision in her left eye with dense floaters. Visual acuity is counting fingers. The red reflex is absent and the retina cannot be seen on fundoscopy. Intraocular pressure is 15 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: When vitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundal view, B-scan ultrasonography is the initial test to check that the retina has not detached.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
No view of the retina = **ultrasound** through the blood.

elim: Less useful than ultrasound for the retina.
Needs a clear view of the retina.
Needs clear media to image the retina.
Will not show whether the retina is attached.

steps.x: **A. B-scan ultrasonography.** Vitreous haemorrhage with no fundal view: B-scan ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has diabetic eye screening. The report reads: 'Right eye R3A M0. Left eye R2 M0.' He has no visual symptoms. His HbA1c is 74 mmol/mol (<42).
questions.q: Which is the most accurate interpretation of the right eye result?
questions.e: R3A is active proliferative retinopathy and needs immediate ophthalmology referral; M0 means no maculopathy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most accurate interpretation of the right eye result? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**R3A** = active new vessels; **M0** = macula fine.

That would be R2 M1.
That would be R0.
That would be R3S.

steps.x: **A. Active proliferative retinopathy without maculopathy.** R3A needs urgent referral even without symptoms.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has R1 M0 retinopathy (microaneurysms only) in both eyes. Her HbA1c is 71 mmol/mol (<42), BP 152/90 mmHg and LDL cholesterol 3.9 mmol/L. Her vision is 6/6.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Optimise glucose, BP and lipids via the GP and continue annual screening
questions.e: Mild NPDR is managed conservatively by tight control of glucose, BP and lipids, referred back to the GP, with continued screening.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Mild NPDR = **risk-factor control** and screening.

elim: No haemorrhage or detachment.
For maculopathy or PDR, not R1.
For severe NPDR or PDR.

steps.x: **C. Optimise glucose, BP and lipids via the GP and continue annual screening.** Prevention: tight glycaemic, BP and lipid control.

questions.stem: A 51 year old taxi driver with type 1 diabetes is about to have pan-retinal laser photocoagulation for proliferative retinopathy in both eyes. He asks what he should be warned about after the treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most important side effect to counsel him about?
o: Loss of central reading vision in most patients
Reduced night vision and peripheral visual field loss
questions.e: PRP destroys ischaemic peripheral retina, reducing VEGF, at the cost of decreased night vision and peripheral field loss in about half of patients, relevant to driving.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most important side effect to counsel him about? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
PRP burns the **periphery**, which holds rods for night and side vision.

elim: Not a typical effect of PRP.
PRP spares the macula.
Not caused by laser.
Laser has no effect on glucose.

steps.x: **E. Reduced night vision and peripheral visual field loss.** PRP side effects: reduced night vision and peripheral field loss (~50%).

questions.stem: A 44 year old man with type 1 diabetes has new vessels on the optic disc and elsewhere in both eyes with a small pre-retinal bleed on the left. Vision is 6/9 in both eyes. There is no macular oedema on OCT.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Observation and repeat screening in 12 months
Urgent pan-retinal laser photocoagulation with intravitreal anti-VEGF
questions.e: PDR needs immediate referral and urgent pan-retinal laser photocoagulation, with intravitreal VEGF inhibitors added for better outcomes.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: new vessels on the optic disc
steps.x: Active new vessels = **PRP** urgently, ± anti-VEGF.

elim: Targets macular oedema, which he does not have.
PDR needs immediate referral and treatment.
Not an inflammatory disease.
Lowers IOP; does not treat neovascularisation.

steps.x: **E. Urgent pan-retinal laser photocoagulation with intravitreal anti-VEGF.** PDR: urgent PRP, anti-VEGF can be added.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has blurred central vision in her left eye. OCT shows central retinal thickening with intraretinal fluid involving the fovea. Visual acuity is 6/24. There are no new vessels. Her HbA1c is 58 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Diabetic maculopathy is treated first-line with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections such as ranibizumab (as for wet AMD).

Centre-involving macular oedema = **anti-VEGF injection**.

elim: Lowers IOP; not a maculopathy treatment.
For PDR; it worsens central vision if used for oedema alone.
Not effective for diabetic macular oedema.
For non-clearing haemorrhage or detachment.

steps.x: **A. Intravitreal ranibizumab.** Maculopathy first line: intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab).

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with treated proliferative retinopathy had a sudden vitreous haemorrhage in his right eye 5 days ago. B-scan ultrasound confirms the retina is attached. Vision is 6/36 and slowly improving. His left eye is 6/6.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management now?
o: Observation, with vitrectomy if it does not clear

No role.
Would worsen bleeding.
Treatment for uveitis.

steps.x: **C. Observation, with vitrectomy if it does not clear.** Vitreous haemorrhage: observe first; vitrectomy if not resolving.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with proliferative diabetic retinopathy has dense fibrovascular membranes. B-scan ultrasound shows a tractional retinal detachment threatening the macula and a large amount of blood in the vitreous. Visual acuity is hand movements.

questions.e: Vitrectomy is indicated when there is a risk of retinal detachment or a large amount of blood in the eye.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

Not inflammatory.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with type 2 diabetes phones his GP surgery. Two hours ago he suddenly lost most of the vision in his left eye with a shower of dark floaters. He had laser treatment for 'new vessels' 2 years ago. He has no pain.

Refer to the optician next week
questions.e: Sudden vision loss in a diabetic suggests vitreous haemorrhage or detachment, an emergency needing immediate ophthalmology referral.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 16 years has tiny round red dots on fundoscopy. Retinal histology from a similar patient shows loss of the cells that wrap around capillaries, with outpouching of the weakened capillary walls.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man with longstanding poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has large areas of capillary non-perfusion on fluorescein angiography. Six months later, new vessels appear at the edges of these areas.

steps.x: **E. Vascular endothelial growth factor.** Ischaemia leads to VEGF and new vessels.
